stem: In which circumstances would you amend your management plan?

options.text: Children aged less than three months

explanation: In a febrile child, the management plan should be escalated or changed if any of these red flags or UTI complexity factors are present. This includes young infants, shock, toxic appearance or vomiting, and atypical, complicated, or recurrent UTI presentations.
rationale: All listed circumstances are indications to amend the usual management plan, so the best answer is the inclusive option.

optionExplanations.A: Infants under 3 months with fever require a different, more urgent assessment and management pathway.
optionExplanations.B: Shock is a red flag requiring immediate escalation and resuscitation.
optionExplanations.C: Toxic appearance or vomiting suggests more severe illness and may change management.
optionExplanations.D: Atypical or complicated UTIs need altered investigation and treatment.
optionExplanations.E: Recurrent UTI requires further assessment and different follow-up.

Instructions

There are 7 questions relating to this scenario.

Clinical scenario 2 - Sarah

Sarah, an 18 month old, presents with a two day history of fever to 39°C. She has no history of cough; rhinorrhoea; vomiting; diarrhoea or rash. She attends day care. She has a 5 year old sibling who is at school and is well at the moment. She is eating less than normal but drinking well and passing urine as normal.

On examination she appears slightly flushed with a fever of 38.5°C. Her HR is 110 and RR 28. Her peripheries are warm and her capillary refill time is 1-2 seconds.

She has no rash, no conjunctivitis, her ENT examination is unremarkable. Her heart sounds are dual with no murmur and her chest is clear. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender. Her immunisations are up to date.

The following seven questions refer to Sarah’s clinical scenario.
